pages.title: Why acid strength follows more than one trend

blocks.text: Hydrogen fluoride has a very polar bond, yet hydroiodic acid is stronger in water. A proton must both be attracted away and overcome its original bond. Bond polarity alone cannot explain every acid-strength trend.

Along a group, increasing atomic size often weakens the H–A bond and favours ionisation. Across a period, increasing electronegativity can increase H–A polarity. Compare like families rather than applying one trend indiscriminately.

pages.transition: Connect those trends to proton removal and conjugate stability.

pages.title: Bond strength and successive proton loss

blocks.text: For the hydrogen halides, the aqueous acid-strength trend is HF < HCl < HBr < HI. Down the group, weakening of the H–halogen bond is important. Across a period the hydrides CH₄, NH₃, H₂O and HF show increasing acidic tendency.
In a polyprotic acid, removing later protons from an increasingly negative ion is less favourable, so successive ionisation constants usually decrease. Each step must be considered separately.

pages.transition: An added ion can suppress ionisation without changing the acid’s K(a).

pages.title: The common-ion effect

blocks.text: The common-ion effect is the suppression of an ionisation equilibrium by adding an electrolyte supplying an ion already present in that equilibrium. It follows from the change in Q and Le Chatelier’s principle.
CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻. Adding sodium ethanoate supplies CH₃COO⁻, raising the product ratio. Net reverse reaction lowers acid ionisation and [H⁺], while K(a) stays fixed at the same temperature.
Common means the same ion appears in both the original equilibrium and the added electrolyte.

pages.transition: A weak acid and its conjugate base can resist a small acid or base addition.

pages.title: A buffer has two chemical partners

blocks.text: A buffer resists a large pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added, and approximately maintains pH on moderate dilution. A typical acidic buffer contains a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A⁻.
Added H⁺ is consumed by A⁻ to form HA. Added OH⁻ is consumed by HA to form A⁻ and water. Both partners must be present in useful amounts; buffer capacity is limited.

pages.transition: The acid equilibrium gives the buffer equation.

pages.title: Derive the acidic-buffer relation

blocks.text: From K(a) = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA], rearrange [H⁺] = K(a)[HA]/[A⁻]. Taking negative base-ten logarithms gives pH = pK(a) + log([A⁻]/[HA]). This is the Henderson–Hasselbalch form in the dilute concentration approximation.
Use the equilibrium acid/base ratio, or the post-reaction amounts when small ionisation corrections can be neglected. Do not insert original amounts before accounting for added strong acid or base.

pages.transition: An equal-ratio example shows what the equation means.

pages.title: Worked buffer calculation

blocks.text: Teacher-created data: pK(a) = 4.76, [HA] = 0.100 M and [A⁻] = 0.100 M. Find pH. Ratio = 1, log 1 = 0, so pH = 4.76. If [A⁻]/[HA] becomes 2, pH = 4.76 + log 2 = 5.06.

Doubling the base-to-acid ratio changes pH by about 0.30, not by a factor of two. Diluting both partners equally leaves their ratio approximately unchanged, but lowers capacity because fewer moles remain per volume.

pages.transition: Basic buffers use the analogous conjugate acid/base pair.

pages.title: Basic-buffer ratios need the right order

blocks.text: For weak base B and conjugate acid BH⁺, K(b) = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B]. Therefore pOH = pK(b) + log([BH⁺]/[B]); equivalently pH = pK(w) − pK(b) + log([B]/[BH⁺]).
NH₃/NH₄⁺ is a basic-buffer pair. With equal concentrations at 298 K, pOH = pK(b) and pH = 14 − pK(b). Reversing the ratio without changing the sign gives the wrong result.

pages.transition: A salt ion can also act as an acid or base when no buffer mixture was deliberately prepared.

pages.title: Salt hydrolysis changes the pH

blocks.text: Hydrolysis here is reaction of a salt ion with water to produce an acidic or basic solution. Ions from a strong acid and strong base, such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻, do not appreciably hydrolyse in ordinary dilute solution.
Acetate hydrolyses: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, giving a basic solution. Ammonium hydrolyses: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺, giving an acidic solution.

pages.transition: Compare both ions if the salt comes from a weak acid and weak base.

pages.title: Which salt ion dominates?

blocks.text: For a weak-acid/weak-base salt, both ions can react with water. The pH depends on the competing acid and base strengths; the word salt does not imply neutrality. A simple dilute treatment gives pH ≈ ½[pK(w) + pK(a) − pK(b)] for suitable conditions.

Teacher-created comparison at 298 K: if pK(a) = 5 and pK(b) = 4, pH ≈ ½(14 + 5 − 4) = 7.5. This is basic because the conjugate-base hydrolysis effect is stronger. The approximation has assumptions and is not a universal concentrated-solution formula.
Buffers work best when both conjugate partners are appreciable. Adding enough strong acid to consume nearly all A⁻ exhausts the buffer even if the starting pH was ideal.

pages.transition: Revise strength trends, common ions, buffers and hydrolysis as related equilibrium applications.

pages.title: Revision: keep the conjugate partner visible

blocks.text: Acid strength reflects bond strength and polarity. Common ions shift an existing equilibrium without changing its constant at fixed temperature. A buffer needs both members of a conjugate pair and has finite capacity.
Acidic buffer: pH = pK(a) + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Basic buffer: pOH = pK(b) + log([BH⁺]/[B]). Salt hydrolysis follows the acid/base behaviour of the ions, not the neutral appearance of the solid.

questions.question: Why does stronger H–F polarity not make HF the strongest hydrogen halide acid?
questions.answer: Bond strength also matters; the strong H–F bond resists dissociation, while bonds weaken down the group.

questions.question: Does added acetate change ethanoic acid’s K(a) at fixed temperature?
questions.answer: No. It changes the composition quotient and suppresses ionisation until the same K(a) is satisfied.

questions.question: Why can pure weak acid alone not buffer added base as effectively as a prepared conjugate mixture?
questions.answer: A useful buffer needs appreciable amounts of both acid and conjugate base to consume added base and acid respectively.

questions.question: If [A⁻]/[HA] = 10, how does pH compare with pK(a)?
Write the correct basic-buffer pOH ratio.
questions.answer: pOH = pK(b) + log([BH⁺]/[B]); conjugate acid is above weak base.

questions.question: Why is NH₄Cl acidic in water?
questions.answer: NH₄⁺ donates a proton to water to form H₃O⁺, while Cl⁻ does not appreciably counteract this by hydrolysis.
